paragraphs.source_en: There is another kind of possible relationship between numerous Round Head paintings and water. In many shelters there are visible traces of ancient waterfalls where rain water left a different colouration of the rock surface, significantly darker or lighter. Since these traces are very neat and evident, the activity of water had to be quite substantial during wet periods and the water course apparently always followed the same track on the wall.

units.source_en: There is another kind of possible relationship between numerous Round Head paintings and water.
In many shelters there are visible traces of ancient waterfalls where rain water left a different colouration of the rock surface, significantly darker or lighter.
Since these traces are very neat and evident, the activity of water had to be quite substantial during wet periods and the water course apparently always followed the same track on the wall.

paragraphs.source_en: In numerous cases Round Head paintings are located next to or below these traces. Traditional thought has assumed that the water erosion on the paintings has been accidental, however, the study of the shelter as a whole, and not limited to the panel itself indicates, that at least in some cases, such situations were by no mean accidental. It is best evident on walls that possess a large surface on which to paint but the paintings are concentrated near the waterfall, leaving the rest of the wall unpainted. I present two cases of this probable relationship in two distinct areas; the first is in the northern Tassili and the second in the Tadrart Acacus.
